appraisal_events.evidence: cette lettre outrageante ... qui avait dû le faire descendre du rang élevé, unique, que par sa bonté, sa loyauté, il avait conquis dans son estime. Il allait lui devenir moins cher.
appraisal_events.explanation: Swann fears that his outrageous letter has toppled him from the elevated place his kindness and loyalty had won in Odette's esteem, believing he will become less dear to her; this is presented as Swann's own anxious surmise rather than a confirmed fact.

appraisal_events.evidence: quelqu'un qui comptait beaucoup dans la vie d'Odette, à qui il était obligé de céder la place, quand ils se rencontraient chez elle ... c'est à Swann qu'elle en aurait su gré.
appraisal_events.explanation: Swann soothes his jealousy by picturing himself as the figure who counts most in Odette's life, with Forcheville obliged to yield to him and any gratitude for her pleasures ultimately redounding to Swann rather than to his rival; this comparative self-elevation is Swann's own consoling rationalization.

status_effects.explanation: Swann's fear that he has lost standing and dearness in Odette's eyes after his outrageous letter marks a local emotional diminishment, though it is his own anxious surmise rather than a confirmed shift in her actual view.
In his consoling counter-reasoning, Swann casts himself as the man who matters most to Odette, with Forcheville obliged to defer to him, restoring some of his sense of standing relative to his rival.
In Swann's imagined reckoning, Forcheville is cast as secondary, obliged to yield to Swann at Odette's and denied credit for any pleasure she might take in his company.

ambiguities: Both appraisal events reflect Swann's own jealous, self-consoling internal reasoning rather than confirmed external judgments by Odette or an objective narrative fact; the passage explicitly frames the second movement as hypothetical ('s'il arrivait que...', 's'il avait approuvé...'), which materially weakens how confidently either shift should be read as real rather than imagined.
